author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This function finds the length of the longest stretch of an array that is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. It walks through `nums` once, comparing each element to the one before it, and keeps three pieces of state: `dir` (the current direction, `'asc'`, `'desc'`, or empty), `count` (the length of the current run), and `max` (the best run seen so far). When the current pair is **increasing**, it extends the run if the direction was already `'asc'`, otherwise it starts a fresh run of length **2** (the two elements being compared) and switches the direction; the **decreasing** case mirrors this with `'desc'`. If two neighbours are **equal**, the run is broken, so `count` resets to **1** and the direction is cleared. After every step `max` is updated with `Math.max`, and since a single element always counts as a monotonic subarray, both `count` and `max` start at **1**. The result is a simple **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space solution.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This version solves the same problem with a clever trick: instead of tracking the direction in a separate variable, it encodes it in the **sign** of `count`. A **positive** `count` means the current run is increasing and a **negative** one means it is decreasing, while `0` means the run was just broken by two equal neighbours. Scanning the array from the second element, if `nums[i - 1] < nums[i]` the code increments `count` when it is already positive (extending an increasing run) or sets it to **2** to start a new one; if `nums[i - 1] > nums[i]` it decrements `count` when already negative or sets it to **-2** to start a new decreasing run. After each step, `max` is updated with `Math.abs(count)` so the sign is stripped and only the run length matters. Both `count` and `max` begin at **1** because any single element is trivially monotonic, and the function returns `max` after a single **O(n)** pass using constant extra space.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution counts **steps** between neighbouring elements rather than elements themselves, which is why it starts `count` and `max` at **0** and returns `max + 1` at the end (a run of `k` consecutive rising or falling steps spans `k + 1` elements, and an array with no steps still has one element). Looping from index 1, it first checks whether the two neighbours are **equal**; if so the run is broken, `count` and `dir` are reset, and `continue` skips straight to the next iteration. Otherwise it determines whether the pair goes `'up'` or `'down'`: if that matches the current `dir`, the run continues and `count` grows by one, but if the direction changed, a new run starts with `count = 1` and `dir` is updated. After each non-equal pair, `max` is refreshed with `Math.max(max, count)`. The approach is a single **O(n)** pass with **O(1)** extra memory.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the most compact version of the idea: it keeps two independent counters, `up` and `down`, that track how many consecutive **rising** and **falling** steps are currently in progress. For every adjacent pair, if the values are **equal** both counters reset to **0** because neither kind of run can continue through a plateau. If the pair is **increasing**, the `down` run is killed by setting it to **0**, `up` is incremented, and `max` is updated with the new `up` value; the **decreasing** case does the opposite, resetting `up` and bumping `down`. Because only one of the two counters can be non-zero at any time, there is no need for a separate direction variable. Like the previous solution, the counters measure steps rather than elements, so the function returns `max + 1` to convert the longest number of steps into the length of the subarray (and to return **1** for a single-element or all-equal array). It runs in **O(n)** time with **O(1)** space.
